newsitem.title: FRANCE: Languedoc-Roussillon durum yields seen down 25 pct.
newsitem.headline: Languedoc-Roussillon durum yields seen down 25 pct.

text.p: Durum yields in Languedoc-Roussillon, France's number one producing area, are expected to fall by at least 25 percent this year due to a prolonged spring drought, local grain officials said on Tuesday.
"The latest yield estimate for the region is 2.7 tonnes per hectare, but it could go lower," an official for the ONIC office in Montpellier said. Last year's yield was 3.6 tonnes.
"Initial fears have been confirmed. This could be the worst crop in at least 10 years," the official added.
Officials and analysts said it was very tricky to make yield predictions while the harvest was still under way because some farmers might not even bother harvesting the worst affected patches.
They linked the yield loss mostly to dry conditions in March and April. Substantial rain in May came too late to help recoup losses.

The harvest started around June 9 and despite steady rain since the middle of the month, farmers have already managed to combine 30 percent of the area. They hoped to complete the harvest by end-June.
Initial data from the fields suggested that the Herault and Gard zones near the Mediteranean sea suffered most, while the Aude region in the west fared better.
Some farmers in the Herault area were reporting yields as low as 2.0 tonnes and the Gard area might not exceed 2.5 tonnes.
The area sown to durum wheat in Languedoc-Roussillon declined to 76,000 hectares this year from 79,000 last year.
Officials said the quality of durum wheat, used to make pasta, appeared to be good and specific weight satisfactory.

Last week crop analysts for the Midi Pyrenees region in the south and the Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region in the southeast predicted the drought might dent local durum yields by more than 25 percent.
The regions rank as France's second and third durum producers.
Soft wheat and barley production are marginal for the region. Farmers sowed 6,100 hectares to soft wheat and 9,900 hectares to barley this year.

The most recent estimates put the average 1997 soft wheat yield at 3.4 tonnes against 3.7 tonnes last year. The drought was expected to push winter barley yields down to 3.3-3.5 tonnes from 4.0 last year.
